claim: The Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 is dated 18 June 1951 ('An Act to amend the Constitution of India'); it was enacted by the Provisional Parliament. The Statement of Objects and Reasons is dated New Delhi, 10 May 1951 and signed by Jawaharlal Nehru.
source: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice: The Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 (with Statement of Objects and Reasons)
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026 (footnotes: w.e.f. 18-6-1951)
note: 'Provisional Parliament' is not printed in the Act's text; it is established by the Shankari Prasad judgment (row 13). The Act's text prints 'Short title... Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951'.

claim: The Statement of Objects and Reasons says that during the last fifteen months of the working of the Constitution, judicial decisions and pronouncements had brought difficulties to light 'specially in regard to the chapter on fundamental rights'.
source: First Amendment Act, Statement of Objects and Reasons
note: [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: claim said "first fifteen months"; the SOR says "last fifteen months of the working". Quote checked.

claim: The SOR says freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) was held by some courts to be so comprehensive as not to make a person culpable even if he advocates murder and other crimes of violence; it adds that other written constitutions do not bar the State from punishing abuse of this freedom.
source: First Amendment Act, Statement of Objects and Reasons
note: Paraphrase; the SOR itself does not name the cases. Romesh Thappar is the case that fits (row 12) but the SOR does not say so.

claim: Section 3 substituted Article 19(2): laws may impose reasonable restrictions on speech and expression 'in the interests of the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence', with retrospective effect ('deemed always to have been enacted'). 'Sovereignty and integrity of India' was added later (Sixteenth Amendment, 1963).
page_or_section: PDF p.2 (s.3(1)(a)); saving of existing laws s.3(2) pp.2-3
second_source: Constitution as on 10 Sep 2026, footnotes to Art 19: First Amendment s.3; Sixteenth Amendment 1963
note: POL03-D02 gives the grounds as they read today. Reuse the id. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: page was p.3; the substituted clause (2) and "deemed always to have been enacted" are on p.2. Text of the grounds checked word for word. Sixteenth Amendment 1963 insertion checked in the Constitution footnote 4 (POL03 source, PDF p.41); that source is not saved in this folder.

claim: Before the amendment, as the Court quoted it in Romesh Thappar, clause (2) saved a law only 'in so far as it relates to any matter which undermines the security of, or tends to overthrow, the State' (plus libel, slander and similar). So 'public order', 'incitement to an offence' and 'friendly relations with foreign States' were new grounds.
source: Romesh Thappar v State of Madras, 26 May 1950, Supreme Court's own copy (judis 1245)
note: The inference that these grounds were 'new' is ours: the original clause (2) is read only as the Court quotes it (omitting 'immaterial words'). The Constitution's own original text (Jan 1950) was not read.

claim: Section 3 also changed Article 19(6): the State may make laws on professional or technical qualifications, and on carrying on a trade, business, industry or service by the State or a State-owned corporation, 'whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise'. The SOR says this puts nationalisation 'beyond doubt'.
source: First Amendment Act, s.3(1)(b) and SOR
note: The SOR wording is 'place the matter beyond doubt' (paraphrased). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: page was pp.1, 3; Art 19(6) text is on p.2. Quotes checked.

claim: Section 2 added Article 15(4): nothing in Article 15 or Article 29(2) shall prevent the State from making special provision for socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for SCs and STs.
note: The SOR says 'article 15(3) should be suitably amplified' and cites Article 46 (directive principle on weaker sections); the Act as passed added a new clause (4), not an amendment of (3). Cite the Act, not the SOR wording.

claim: Sections 4-5 inserted Article 31A (laws for acquiring estates or rights in them are not void for inconsistency with Part III; a State law needs the President's assent) and Article 31B (the Acts in the Ninth Schedule are not void on that ground, 'notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court', subject to the legislature's power to repeal or amend). Section 14 added the Ninth Schedule with 13 entries (zamindari and tenure abolition laws of Bihar, Bombay, Madhya Pradesh, Madras, Uttar Pradesh and Hyderabad).
page_or_section: PDF p.3 (Arts 31A, 31B); pp.5-6 (Ninth Schedule, entries 1-7 on p.5, 8-13 on p.6)
note: Entry 1 is the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. 13 counted by us from the Schedule text. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: pages were pp.3-5. Thirteen entries recounted; entry 1 Bihar; states Bihar, Bombay, Madhya Pradesh, Madras, Uttar Pradesh, Hyderabad confirmed.

claim: The SOR says the validity of agrarian reform laws passed by State legislatures in the previous three years had been held up by 'dilatory litigation', so the Bill sought to secure zamindari abolition laws.
source: First Amendment Act, Statement of Objects and Reasons

claim: Other changes: Articles 85 and 174 (six months shall not intervene between sessions; President/Governor may prorogue and dissolve), Articles 87 and 176 (address at first session after each general election and at the first session of each year), Articles 341 and 342 (consultation with the Governor or Rajpramukh now only where the State is in Part A or Part B), Article 372 (two years to three), Article 376 (non-citizen High Court judges eligible to be Chief Justice).
note: [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX: pages were pp.5-6 (ss.6-9 are on p.4, ss.10-14 start on p.5). The 341/342 gloss "Presidential notification" described the article, not the change; replaced by the actual change in the Act.

claim: State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan (judgment 9 Apr 1951; seven judges): the 'Communal G.O.' fixing seats for communities in State engineering and medical colleges violated Article 29(2), so was void under Article 13; the directive principles in Part IV cannot override fundamental rights in Part III ('the chapter of Fundamental Rights is sacrosanct'); appeals dismissed.
source: State of Madras v Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan, 1951 AIR 226, 1951 SCR 525, Supreme Court's own copy (judis 1194)
page_or_section: headnote PDF pp.1-2; 'sacrosanct' p.5; order p.6
second_source: POL03-B05 (links Art 15(4) to Champakam via Indra Sawhney)
note: The Court's reasoning is Art 29(2); the quoted 'Art 16(4)' in its heading is a cited provision. The First Amendment's Art 15(4) reaches Art 29(2) too ('or in clause (2) of article 29'). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] FIX (labelling): the link between Champakam and the First Amendment's Art 15(4) is our inference (via Indra Sawhney as reported in POL03-B05, which was not opened here); the Act's SOR cites Art 46 and names no case. Judgment date, 7-judge bench, "sacrosanct" (p.5) and "Appeals dismissed" (p.6) verified at the Court's copy.

claim: Romesh Thappar v State of Madras (26 May 1950): the Court (Patanjali Sastri J. for Kania CJ, Mahajan, Mukherjea and Das JJ.) held s.9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 wholly unconstitutional and void, because restrictions for 'public order' fall outside what Article 19(2) then authorised; Fazl Ali J. dissented; petition allowed. (Bench read from the headnote: Kania CJ, Sastri, Mahajan, Mukherjea, Das JJ. in the majority.)
value: Thappar: public order outside 19(2); law void
source: Romesh Thappar v State of Madras, AIR 1950 SC 124, 1950 SCR 594, Supreme Court's own copy (judis 1245)
note: The saved PDF's header lists Fazl Ali first; the bench split is read from the headnote. The link 'Thappar led to the amendment' is our inference (the SOR does not name the case).

claim: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v Union of India (5 Oct 1951; Patanjali Sastri, Kania CJ, Mukherjea, S.R. Das and Aiyar JJ.): the First Amendment Act was not ultra vires; the Provisional Parliament could exercise the amending power under Article 368; 'law' in Article 13(2) means ordinary legislative power, not constituent power, so Art 13(2) does not bar amendments; petitions dismissed with costs.
source: Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v Union of India, 1951 AIR 458, 1952 SCR 89, Supreme Court's own copy (judis 1174)
note: The Court expressly gave no opinion on whether the latter part of Art 31B was too widely expressed (not argued), p.13. Overruled for the future in Golaknath (1967): POL06-C04.

claim: I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu (11 Jan 2007; nine judges, Sabharwal CJI): laws placed in the Ninth Schedule on or after 24 April 1973 can be challenged if they destroy or damage the basic structure, tested by the 'rights test' and 'essence of the right' test; laws already upheld by the Court cannot be re-challenged on these principles.
value: Coelho: post-24 Apr 1973 Ninth Schedule laws reviewable
source: I.R. Coelho (Dead) by LRs v State of Tamil Nadu, Supreme Court's own copy (judis 28469)
note: Waman Rao (1980) is the 24 Apr 1973 cut-off source, POL06-F06 (mirror). Bench listed in the saved header is nine names.
